summary:
Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres: the Chueca district is the community's epicentre, the annual Pride event (MADO) in late June or early July draws millions of attendees, and daily life offers substantial anonymity for LGBT visitors. The same source records that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in the city, and that marginalised groups including trans people and migrants face additional barriers.

The national framework a visitor's documents stand under is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The statute also carries broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy. Human Rights Watch described it in February 2023 as a hard-won victory after years of activism.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Courts apply the aggravation in practice: in Vigo a Tribunal de Instancia used it for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300; in Valencia a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia, after Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute sits above the national floor set by Ley 4/2023 and was amended by Ley 17/2023. On 27 December 2023 two community laws, Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023, amended the 2016 gender-identity law and the regional anti-LGBTBI law on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, stripping the provisions that obliged educational institutions; the resulting restrictions sit in the school environment and do not touch a visitor's public conduct, documents or entry.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and the country is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly in the world.
tangentialFactors:
Madrid's 2016 statute made the community one of the earliest in Spain to legislate gender identity directly, moving in parallel with the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and one year after Extremadura; the national Ley 4/2023 now sets the floor those regional statutes must satisfy.

With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Local support infrastructure includes COGAM, founded in 1986 and the city's most influential LGBT organisation, the city government's Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género, and Arcopoli, which works against discrimination and violence.

Madrid Pride (MADO) is described as one of the largest Pride events in the world, and Madrid itself as one of Europe's main LGBT hubs, which bears on how visible a trans visitor will be in public space.
localsOnly:
The regional 2016 gender-identity law and the regional anti-LGBTBI law are the statutes a resident interacts with locally. Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023 of 27 December 2023 amended both, on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, removing the provisions that obliged educational institutions.

Ley 4/2023 regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of gender identity is possible from age 12 under conditions.

The national law carries employment and health measures and requires an LGTBI equality strategy, which apply to residents throughout the community.

Transphobic motivation as an aggravating circumstance and the Article 510 hate offences are criminal-law tools available to residents as complainants, alongside the reformed offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a prosecution under Article 510 of the Criminal Code arising in the Comunidad de Madrid. The two applications of the aggravating circumstance on record are from Vigo and Valencia, so the frequency of such cases in this community is unresolved.

Whether the 2023 community amendments have affected any facility-access dispute, document request or police interaction in the Comunidad de Madrid is not sourced here.

The full text of Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023 has not been independently reviewed for this record; the description of their scope rests on the summary carried in the source inventory.

No visitor-specific data on hate-crime reporting rates, or on how gender-marker mismatches are handled at Madrid airports, hotels or medical facilities, is available in the inventory.
